name: Mulholland Drive (2001)
teaser: Lynch's film — a woman with amnesia, an aspiring actress, and a Hollywood dream that curdles into nightmare — began as a TV pilot that was rejected, then was reshot and re-edited into a feature that won the Palme d'Or and became one of the most analyzed films ever made. Its 'Silencio' club scene is the film's thesis in performance.

exploreAction.targetName: Mulholland Drive (2001) — the Silencio scene and the ending
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the limousine, the accident, the woman who walks away from the wreck with a purse of cash — and notice how Lynch withholds meaning: the film's first half is a dream that never explains itself, and the mystery is the pleasure.

name: Lost in Translation (2003)
teaser: Coppola's film — two lonely Americans in a Tokyo hotel, a fading actor and a recent bride, who find each other in the small hours — was shot in 27 days and won the Oscar for Best Original Screenplay, making Coppola the third woman to be nominated for Best Director. Its ending, a whispered goodbye in a crowded street, is one of the most imitated final scenes in cinema.

exploreAction.targetName: Lost in Translation (2003) — the karaoke night and the ending
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the taxi ride through neon Tokyo, the jet lag, the first glimpse of Bob's hotel window — and notice how Coppola films loneliness: the film's Tokyo is a city of signs Bob can't read, and the silence is the dialogue.

name: Brokeback Mountain (2005)
teaser: Lee's film — two cowboys whose one summer in the Wyoming mountains becomes a twenty-year secret — won three Oscars including Best Director, and its story of Ennis and Jack changed how Hollywood told queer stories. Its famous line — 'I wish I knew how to quit you' — became shorthand for the film's refusal to let its characters be simple.

exploreAction.targetName: Brokeback Mountain (2005) — the reunion and the ending
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the sheep, the first campfire, the tent — and notice how Lee films the affair: the film's landscapes are as important as its faces, and the love story is told in glances across a valley.

name: Children of Men (2006)
teaser: Cuarón's film — set in 2027, when humanity has been infertile for 18 years and a pregnant woman appears — was shot in a London that looks like a war zone, with several action sequences filmed in single unbroken takes. Its central argument — that hope is the last political act — made it the definitive dystopia of its decade.

exploreAction.targetName: Children of Men (2006) — the single-take battle sequence
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the café, the news report, the explosion — and notice how Cuarón establishes the world: the film's future is the present run on, and every set piece is a descent into a world that has stopped caring.

name: A Serious Man (2009)
teaser: The Coens' film — a physics professor in 1967 Minnesota whose life collapses in a series of Job-like trials, from his wife's affair to a tenure fight — is their most personal film, drawn from their own Jewish upbringing in a Minneapolis suburb. Its opening parable, set in a shtetl in an indeterminate past, sets the film's whole argument in three minutes.

exploreAction.targetName: A Serious Man (2009) — the opening parable and the ending
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the dybbuk, the visitor, the man stabbed in the chest who walks in and says 'help me' — and notice how the Coens set the frame: the parable is the film's thesis, and everything that follows is a modern retelling.

name: Inception (2010)
teaser: Nolan's film — a thief who enters people's dreams to steal ideas, hired for the reverse: planting one — was a $160 million puzzle box that grossed $830 million and won four Oscars, and its rotating-corridor fight became one of the great images of 2010s cinema. Its final shot, a spinning top that may or may not fall, launched a decade of debate.

exploreAction.targetName: Inception (2010) — the corridor fight and the ending
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the beach, the old man, the top — and notice how Nolan establishes the film's rules: the film is a heist movie about architecture, and every level of the dream is a new scale of time. Then watch the corridor fight, where the physics of the dream are renegotiated mid-scene: the film's argument — that an idea can be the most dangerous weapon, and that reality is a matter of faith — is dramatized in the three-level climax.

name: A Separation (2011)
teaser: Farhadi's film — an Iranian couple's divorce, a caregiver's fall, and a legal case that exposes every character's compromise — won the Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film and became the most honored Iranian film ever made. Its genius is that every character is both right and wrong, and the audience is the jury.

exploreAction.targetName: A Separation (2011) — the trial scenes and the ending
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the couple's divorce petition, the judge's office, the first exchange about what each wants — and notice how Farhadi builds the film from a single decision: the divorce is the engine, and every scene is a new piece of the case.

name: Amour (2012)
teaser: Haneke's film — an elderly Parisian couple, and the wife's stroke that turns their love into a slow, unbearable caregiving — won the Palme d'Or and the Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film, and Emmanuelle Riva became the oldest Best Actress nominee in history. Its title is French for 'love,' and its final act is the hardest examination of what that word means.

exploreAction.targetName: Amour (2012) — the opening and the final act
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the locked door, the police, the body laid out in the apartment — and notice how Haneke starts with the ending: the film is a flashback to the ordinary life that preceded the tragedy, and the camera's calm is the horror.

name: Gravity (2013)
teaser: Cuarón's film — an astronaut stranded in orbit after her shuttle is destroyed — was shot as one long, floating ballet of survival, and won seven Oscars for its craft, with the 13-minute single-take opening becoming the film's signature. It grossed $700 million and made space look, for the first time, both beautiful and lethal.

exploreAction.targetName: Gravity (2013) — the opening and the re-entry sequence
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the shuttle's silent ballet, the music, the first sight of the debris cloud — and notice how Cuarón establishes the film's physics: there is no sound in space, and the film's silence is its terror.

name: Whiplash (2014)
teaser: Chazelle's film — a young drummer and the tyrannical jazz teacher who abuses him into greatness — won three Oscars including Best Supporting Actor for J.K. Simmons, and its final drum solo, filmed in real time, became one of the great climaxes in cinema. Its central question — is greatness worth the damage? — is never answered.

exploreAction.targetName: Whiplash (2014) — the final performance
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the practice room, the first confrontation, the chair thrown at Andrew's head — and notice how Chazelle establishes the film's stakes: the film is about perfection as a form of abuse, and every scene is a negotiation of that abuse.

name: Get Out (2017)
teaser: Peele's debut — a Black photographer meeting his white girlfriend's family, who turn out to be operating a sinister scheme — became the most profitable film of 2017 and the definitive 'social thriller,' winning Peele the Oscar for Best Original Screenplay. Its 'sunken place' became an instant cultural metaphor.

exploreAction.targetName: Get Out (2017) — the sunken place and the ending
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the suburban street at night, the abduction, the deer — and notice how Peele establishes the film's grammar: every polite gesture in the film is a threat, and the film's horror is in the compliments.

name: Dune (2021)
teaser: Villeneuve's adaptation of Frank Herbert's novel — the first of two parts — brought the desert planet Arrakis to the screen with a scale no previous version managed, winning six Oscars and grossing $400 million in a pandemic year. Its 'voice' sequences and sandworm rides made it the defining epic of the decade.

exploreAction.targetName: Dune (2021) — the sandworm sequences
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the voiceover, the desert, the first sight of the sandworm — and notice how Villeneuve establishes Arrakis: the film is about ecology and prophecy, and every scene of the desert is a lesson in Herbert's world-building.

name: The Power of the Dog (2021)
teaser: Campion's film — a rancher in 1925 Montana who torments his brother's new wife and forms a twisted bond with her son — won the Oscar for Best Director, making Campion the third woman and first New Zealander to win, and was nominated for 12 Oscars overall. Its twist, withheld for two hours, reframes the entire film.

exploreAction.targetName: The Power of the Dog (2021) — the ending reveal
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the cattle drive, the rope, Phil's cruelty to the new wife — and notice how Campion films the western: the film's landscapes are psychological, and Phil's rage is the film's engine.

name: Tár (2022)
teaser: Field's film — the fictional conductor Lydia Tár, the first woman to lead the Berlin Philharmonic, whose past abuses catch up with her — was Cate Blanchett's most celebrated performance, earning her the Venice Volpi Cup and an Oscar nomination. Its central question — what do we owe the artists whose work we love, if they are monsters? — is never resolved.

exploreAction.targetName: Tár (2022) — the Juilliard scene and the unraveling
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the New Yorker-style interview, the Juilliard class, the conductor's godlike confidence — and notice how Field builds the film from Tár's control: the film is a portrait of power, and every scene is a scene of Tár managing perception.

name: Sholay (1975)
teaser: Ramesh Sippy's 1975 dacoit-western fusion that redefined the Bollywood blockbuster — the highest-grossing Indian film for two decades. Amjad Khan's Gabbar Singh was a last-minute casting gamble; his growl came from a prosthetic jaw.

exploreAction.targetName: Sholay (1975) — the first hour
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the first hour and count how many times the plot turns on a line of dialogue instead of a gunfight. Notice how Sippy shoots the Thakur-Gabbar confrontation like a Leone western — wide frames, dust, silence — then cuts to melodrama the instant the music starts.

name: Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge (1995)
teaser: 1995 — still running at Mumbai's Maratha Mandir decades later, a world record for theatrical longevity. Shah Rukh Khan's Raj made the NRI love story a genre; the mustard-field finale became Indian cinema's most imitated image.

exploreAction.targetName: Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge (1995) — the first hour
exploreAction.instruction: Notice how the first hour delays the couple's first meeting for twenty minutes — the film knows anticipation is the plot. Then watch 'Tujhe Dekha Toh' twice: the lyrics, the wind machine, the train — every frame sells a love you never see consummated.

name: Lagaan (2001)
teaser: 2001 — India's third Oscar nomination for Best Foreign Language Film. A drought-stricken village bets its taxes on a cricket match against the British Raj; the cast trained with real cricketers, and Aamir Khan learned left-hand batting for one role.

exploreAction.targetName: Lagaan (2001) — the first hour
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the film turns a colonial tax dispute into a siege. The villagers' practice montage matters: every bungled catch pays off in the final innings. The match is filmed in real time — no cuts mid-delivery, so the umpire's calls become the drama.

name: 3 Idiots (2009)
teaser: 2009 — the highest-grossing Indian film of its decade. Rajkumar Hirani's takedown of rote education stars Aamir Khan as a genius who asks 'why' instead of 'what'; the 'All Izz Well' scooter scene was filmed with Khan genuinely unable to control the bike.

exploreAction.targetName: 3 Idiots (2009) — the first hour
exploreAction.instruction: Notice how every lecture scene is staged like a courtroom — the professor prosecutes, Rancho defends with questions. The hostel raid is one long tracking shot. Hirani hides the film's argument inside gags: the 'machine' monologue is the thesis.

name: Dangal (2016)
teaser: 2016 — China's biggest foreign-language hit in history. Aamir Khan gained 25kg to play the ageing father, then shed it for the flashbacks; the real Phogat sisters coached the actresses. The wrestling is filmed in unbroken takes — no cuts mid-match.

exploreAction.targetName: Dangal (2016) — the first hour
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the wrestling scenes for the sound design: every throw lands with a wet thud before the crowd reacts. The first hour builds the daughters' rebellion, then the haircut scene flips the mood — notice how the music stops at the barber's chair.

name: Pyaasa (1957)
teaser: Guru Dutt's 1957 portrait of a poet crushed by a world that buys and sells words — routinely ranked among the greatest films ever made. 'Jaane Woh Kaise Log The' was filmed in one unbroken take through the streets of a sleeping city.

exploreAction.targetName: Pyaasa (1957) — the first hour
exploreAction.instruction: Watch 'Jaane Woh Kaise Log The' without reading the subtitles — the camera does the talking. Dutt films Vijay's poems as private objects, then the market scenes turn the same words into currency. That exchange is the whole film.

name: Mughal-e-Azam (1960)
teaser: 1960 — fifteen years in the making and the most expensive Indian film of its era. 'Pyar Kiya To Darna Kya' was shot in a palace of mirrored glass; one war scene used over a hundred thousand extras. A 2004 re-release colorized scenes shot in black-and-white.

exploreAction.targetName: Mughal-e-Azam (1960) — the Sheesh Mahal sequence
exploreAction.instruction: Skip ahead to the Sheesh Mahal — the mirrored hall where 'Pyar Kiya To Darna Kya' is sung. Anarkali's defiance is framed in shattered reflections: the mirror splits her into many selves while the emperor listens. Then watch the war scene and count the extras.

name: Mother India (1957)
teaser: 1957 — the first Indian film nominated for a Best Foreign Language Oscar. Nargis's Radha became the archetypal Indian mother; she nearly drowned filming the flood sequence. The title deliberately echoed Maxim Gorky's 'Mother'.

exploreAction.targetName: Mother India (1957) — the first hour
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the flood scene knowing it was filmed with a real surge — Nargis was nearly swept away. The film's engine is Birju's resentment: every time the camera frames Radha's hands in the soil, it's foreshadowing the final act's shovel.

name: Deewaar (1975)
teaser: 1975 — the film that codified Bollywood's 'angry young man'. Amitabh Bachchan's 'Mere paas maa hai' is among the most quoted lines in Indian cinema; Yash Chopra shot the confrontation in one long take to let the silence build.

exploreAction.targetName: Deewaar (1975) — the first hour
exploreAction.instruction: The film is built on brothers choosing opposite sides of the law. Watch the 'Mere paas maa hai' scene and notice the blocking: both brothers refuse to move and the camera never cuts — the standoff is physical before it's verbal.

name: Shree 420 (1955)
teaser: Raj Kapoor's 1955 tramp-in-the-city satire — 'Mera Joota Hai Japani' became the anthem of post-independence India. The title is slang for a con man, after the penal code's Section 420; Kapoor's Chaplin-esque tramp walked the line between them.

exploreAction.targetName: Shree 420 (1955) — the first hour
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening song: Raj's tramp walks into Bombay singing 'Mera Joota Hai Japani' — the whole film's argument in one chorus. Then notice how the same shoes become the metaphor for selling out when he trades them for a suit.
